open_questions: The hi-hat lift on 2 and 4: Wikipedia dates it from about 1969 and he confirms the habit (to Mattingly), but the human Songsterr tabs read for this record write the hats through the backbeat on every song from 1965 to 1981. Which records show it, and how often, wants the records' stems or close footage, not the tabs.
The late backbeat (Wikipedia: about 1968 to the mid-1970s, 'Monkey Man', 'Wild Horses') is not measured here; the style's snare lag is a guess at its size.

Read the Modern Drummer interviews (Max Weinberg, The Big Beat, 1984; Modern Drummer cover stories) and Chet Falzerano's Charlie Watts' Favorite Drummers (2012) for his heroes in his own words: Phil Seamen, Kenny Clarke, Papa Jo Jones and Jerry Allison are in that book's list, which was read only in a review.

Boing Boing (2021) on 'how to drum like Charlie Watts' could not be read (403): its quote, 'I think the reason I did it is to get the hand out of the way to do a bigger backbeat', is from a 2018 video interview not traced.

Sympathy for the Devil: the human tab (52286) has only the kick in quarters and the hat foot on the 'and's; NPR hears a cross-stick on a snare with its snares off. Not written as a song until that is settled.

Which kit on which record after 1968: the tabs name a Gretsch in Black Nitron, a Name Band in Black Diamond Pearl and the natural maple round badge; only the Black Nitron (1968) and the maple (1978) are dated by Wikipedia.

identity.name: Charlie Watts
home_scenes: The London jazz clubs and Alexis Korner's Blues Incorporated (1961 to 1962)
The Ealing Jazz Club and the Rolling Stones (from January 1963)
identity.summary: The Rolling Stones' drummer for fifty-eight years, from January 1963 to his death, and a jazzman who never wanted to be anything else: a Chico Hamilton and Charlie Parker fan who took the neck off a banjo to play its head as a snare. A song drummer with no solos and few fills: the snare a shade late, the right hand lifted off the hats for a bigger backbeat, the band following Keith Richards rather than the drums, and records built on one plain groove held for three minutes (Satisfaction, Jumpin' Jack Flash, Start Me Up).

formation.first_instrument: banjo head played as a snare

traditions.impact: His first records were jazz 78s, Jelly Roll Morton and Charlie Parker; 'The first thing I heard that I wanted to emulate was Chico Hamilton playing brushes on "Walkin' Shoes" by Gerry Mulligan.' He practised along to jazz records and played with London jazz bands at night.

traditions.tradition: Chicago blues and R&B, through Korner and Richards
traditions.impact: Blues Incorporated from 1961; after he joined the Stones, Richards gave him a crash course in blues and early rock and roll. Of Jimmy Reed's drummer Earl Phillips: he 'kind of played like a jazz drummer'.

formative_events.event: A GBP 12 drum kit for Christmas, after a banjo with its neck taken off had served as a snare.
Alexis Korner asks him into Blues Incorporated, with Jack Bruce and Dick Heckstall-Smith; he keeps a day job in advertising.
Joins the Rolling Stones in January 1963 in Tony Chapman's place, suggesting Ginger Baker for his own chair in Blues Incorporated.
Plays matched grip 'for a few years, because I thought it was popular'; Ian Stewart 'virtually ordered me to go back to ... the "proper" way of playing'.

eras.label: London jazz and Blues Incorporated
eras.context: Art school and advertising by day, jazz bands at night; Alexis Korner and Cyril Davies's Blues Incorporated at the Ealing Club.

eras.label: The Stones' singles (Ludwig)
eras.context: Andrew Loog Oldham's Stones: R&B covers, then the Jagger-Richards singles cut at RCA in Hollywood, Satisfaction, Get Off of My Cloud, Paint It Black.
defining_traits: four on the snare under eighths
the floor tom as a march

eras.label: The Jimmy Miller years (Gretsch)
eras.context: Jimmy Miller produces Jumpin' Jack Flash to Goats Head Soup; Mick Taylor in Brian Jones's place from 1969; Let It Bleed, Sticky Fingers, Exile on Main St.
defining_traits: the hand lifted off the hats on 2 and 4
eras.style_shift: From about 1969 he left out the hi-hat on the backbeat, and from about 1968 to the mid-1970s often laid the snare a little late (Wikipedia).

eras.label: Some Girls to the stadiums
eras.context: Ronnie Wood in the band from 1975; Some Girls (1978), Tattoo You (1981); the stadium tours; less acceleration in the studio after the mid-1970s (Wikipedia).
defining_traits: the plainest beat held for a whole song (Start Me Up)

eras.label: His own jazz bands
eras.context: Rocket 88 with Ian Stewart; the Charlie Watts Orchestra (1980s); the Quintet (Warm and Tender, 1993); the Tentet; the Charlie Watts Jim Keltner Project (2000); the ABC&D of Boogie Woogie (from 2009).

genres.notes: The early Stones' R&B covers; Miss You's four on the floor.
His first love and his own bands; he never claimed to be a jazz drummer 'in a book that you ring up'.

evidence.note: Wikipedia: from about 1968 to the mid-1970s he often delayed the snare slightly on 2 and 4. Not measured here.

swing.notes: Straight eighths on every record read here (the cymbal band and the tabs); 'it should swing and bounce' is his word for the feel, not a swing ratio. Tumbling Dice drags rather than shuffles.

dynamics.balance: A strong backbeat, louder for the right hand coming off the hats; few ghost notes; quiet cymbals, the crash at the tops of sections.

feel_profile.interaction: He follows Keith Richards rather than leading: Richards's amp was set by his hi-hat so he could hear it, and the tempo breathes with the guitar ('come up a little bit in tempo here, and then it should pull back there'). Kakutani: this is what 'makes the Stones impossible to copy'.

hand_techniques.name: The hand off the hat
hand_techniques.description: The right hand lifts off the hi-hat as the left plays the backbeat: 'I was never conscious of doing it until Jim Keltner mentioned it ... I suppose I got in the habit of pulling the stick out of the way to get a louder sound.' From about 1969 (Wikipedia).

hand_techniques.name: Traditional grip
hand_techniques.description: Matched grip for a few years in the 1960s 'because I thought it was popular', then back to 'the military grip' at Ian Stewart's insistence: 'I really do prefer it.'

hand_techniques.name: Brushes
hand_techniques.description: 'My love was rhythm brushes - wire brushes'; one of the few rock drummers to use them on some songs.

foot_techniques.name: The hat opened and closed with the foot
foot_techniques.description: The hat opened on an 'and' and closed with the foot on the next beat (Tumbling Dice, Beast of Burden, Miss You's chorus on every 'and').

rudiments.name: Single stroke roll
rudiments.application: Short runs of sixteenths on the snare at the end of a line (Get Off of My Cloud, Start Me Up, Tumbling Dice).

coordination.notes: Ostinato in the sense of one groove held through a whole record (Satisfaction, Jumpin' Jack Flash, Start Me Up).

devices_search.note: None found. The leads that did not hold: the hand lifted off the hat on 2 and 4 is an omission in the ostinato, not a second pulse; Tumbling Dice's fills in sextuplets subdivide the beat in six, a lick, not a cross-rhythm; Paint It Black's floor tom in eighths under the snare on every beat is one pulse doubled; nothing in the tabs runs an accent cycle across the bar.

voice_language.snare: The backbeat on 2 and 4, a shade late, bigger for the right hand coming off the hat; on every beat for Satisfaction and choruses; accented through Brown Sugar; short runs of sixteenths at the ends of lines.
voice_language.kick: Plain: 1 and 3 (Start Me Up), or following the riff, the 'and' of 2 (Jumpin' Jack Flash), the 'and's of 3 and 4 (Honky Tonk Women); every beat for Miss You.
voice_language.toms: The floor tom in eighths as a march (Paint It Black) or a groove (Brown Sugar's verses); Gimme Shelter's paired sixteenths round the snare and two toms.
voice_language.hihat: Eighths, washy and half-open in the 1960s, opened on an 'and' and closed with the foot; the hand off it on the backbeat.
voice_language.cymbals: Few: a crash at the top of a section; the ride for Gimme Shelter's intro and a verse of Get Off of My Cloud.
voice_language.percussion: Producers and friends play the cowbell, maracas and congas beside him (Jimmy Miller, Rocky Dijon).

implements.notes: Brushes in his jazz bands and on some Stones songs.

tuning.snare: Medium, with the wires on; a Ludwig Supraphonic in the 1960s (as the Paint It Black tab names it).
tuning.toms: One rack tom and one floor tom, open.

sound_profile.muffling: Not documented in the sources read.
sound_profile.cymbal_character: A hi-hat and four cymbals on the 1978 kit; on film at Hyde Park, 1969, a crash beside the hats.

by_era.description: Ludwig drums in a small room at RCA Hollywood; washy hats.
The Gretsch in Black Nitron; Olympic, Muscle Shoals and Nellcôte's basement, close and dry.
The late-1950s Gretsch round badge in natural maple, Pathé Marconi's dry drums on Some Girls.

sample_hints.sixties: A 1960s Ludwig, ringing toms, washy thin cymbals.
sample_hints.seventies: A small Gretsch, round and warm, short dark cymbals.

signature_traits.label: The hand off the hat on 2 and 4
signature_traits.description: The right hand leaves the hi-hat as the left plays the backbeat, so the snare speaks louder and alone: 'pulling the stick out of the way to get a louder sound'. From about 1969; Jim Keltner pointed it out to him.

signature_traits.label: The late backbeat
signature_traits.description: The snare slightly delayed on 2 and 4, from about 1968 to the mid-1970s ('Monkey Man', 'Wild Horses').

signature_traits.label: Following the guitar
signature_traits.description: The band follows Keith Richards, and Watts follows him too, the tempo coming up and pulling back with the song; often faster by the end, most of all in Honky Tonk Women (about 115 to 125 on the record).

signature_traits.label: One groove for the whole record
signature_traits.description: Satisfaction's snare and kick on every beat, Jumpin' Jack Flash's kick on the 'and' of 2, Start Me Up's 1 and 3: one bar held from the first verse to the fade, with almost no fills and no solos ('I don't like drum solos').

signature_traits.label: The floor tom as a groove
signature_traits.description: Eighths on the floor tom in place of the hats: a march under the snare on every beat in Paint It Black, the verse of Brown Sugar under an accented backbeat.

philosophy.idea: Make it a dance sound: it should swing and bounce.
Play with the band, not over it: no drum solos.
The drummer is the engine, and the tempo breathes with the song: up a little here, pulled back there.

innovations: The hand lifted off the hi-hat for a bigger, cleaner backbeat

Jazz restraint and a jazz kit in the biggest rock band

cultural_references.description: Robert Christgau: 'rock's greatest drummer'. Keith Richards: 'you suddenly realize that you're floating a few inches off the ground.'

common_misconceptions: That he drums on all of Tumbling Dice: Jimmy Miller plays the coda.
That the Stones follow the drummer: Watts follows Keith Richards.

beatbreaker.default_kit_sound: A small 1960s Ludwig or Gretsch, round and warm, short dark cymbals
generation_rules: Straight eighths, the snare a shade late; the kick plain (1 and 3) or on the riff's own rhythm.
The right hand often off the hats on 2 and 4.
One groove held through a section; a crash at its top, few fills and those short (a few sixteenths on the snare, a pair of toms).
The floor tom in eighths in place of the hats for a march or a verse.
No solos, no tom runs round the kit, no china.
